references.cited_text: THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C106 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ There's a particular kind of week in this city where nothing breaks open and everything still shifts. Y2C106 was that kind of week. The gray hasn't lifted — Noah Tan reported from Lake Merritt on a third consecutive week of overcast skies that have done something to the social fabric of that neighborhood, and it's not a small thing. Toby Lamont told Noah he felt the whole rhythm change. Mina Linas, who monitors the lake and sees who stops and who keeps walking, said even the regulars just nod now and move on. A city under low clouds is still a city, but it operates differently — more interior, more private, more provisional. The benches stay empty. People are waiting for something to break, as Tobi Sobi put it from her kitchen table, watching her kids lose enthusiasm for the outside world.

Start with the A's, because the city already has. Hal Richmond put it the right way when he reached for the word "absurdity" to describe a 127-win season — not as an insult but as the only accurate measurement. Benji Dillon threw five and a third innings. Vinnie Keane went four-for-five. Mark Aitken hit two home runs and drove in six. These are numbers that belong in a conversation about memory, not a box score. Richmond was standing on Broadway watching confetti stick to streetcar rails after the 2035 championship, and this week he was watching a team that made that squad look modest. Keane, talking to Richmond afterward, was almost too quiet about it — "coming together as a team," he said, voice steady, which is the kind of understatement you earn at 127 wins. What I keep turning over is Richmond's closing note: stories like this always have endings, and the question is how we'll remember this team when the confetti is gone. That's the right question. We're just not there yet.

By Hal Richmond | Bay Tribune Sports The Rhythm of Late Seasons By Hal Richmond The Oakland A’s won again last night. They always seem to win these days. One hundred twenty-seven times this season, in fact, and counting. The box score reads like a symphony: Benji Dillon’s five and a third innings, eight strikeouts, two hits; Vinnie Keane’s four-for-five with a home run, a double, three RBI; Mark Aitken’s two homers, six runs batted in. The streak grows to two, the record bloats to absurdity, and the city hums with the kind of late-season electricity that feels both inevitable and fleeting.

“I feel like we’re really coming together as a team,” Keane said afterward, his voice steady, his words measured. “I’m seeing some great performances from my teammates. It’s an exciting time to be an A’s player.” Keane’s line feels almost understated, a quiet acknowledgment of the machine this team has become. Yet underneath the calm, there’s a weight to his tone—a recognition, perhaps, that this kind of dominance is rare, even for a franchise as storied as Oakland’s. Mark Aitken felt it too, the energy of late-season games where every pitch and every swing seem to carry the weight of something larger. “It’s exciting to see them perform at this level,” he said, nodding toward his teammates.

The Oaks came up twice too, and in ways that don't quite match. Talia Finch went to West Oakland and found Elio Perez and Daniel Cloak and Darius Clark all saying, with genuine warmth, that the team is reaching toward the community and that it matters. Then Simon Leary spent his week with the A's record — 127-35, a machine more than a team by now — and asked the harder question: at what point does the architecture become the story, rather than the people passing through? Martin Richards, a veteran who knows something about being moved across positions and cities, told Simon that value shifts sometimes overnight. Ollie Campbell, who doesn't even follow sports closely, noticed people talking about how the A's keep winning no matter who's holding the beams. The Oaks engagement Talia documented and the A's apparatus Simon examined are two different models of what a sports franchise can be in this city. One is still trying to be recognized by its neighborhood. The other has achieved something so structural it barely needs anyone's recognition.

Down the road, somewhere an engine wasn’t running, Ollie Campbell considered it all from a distance. “I don’t follow sports much,” they admitted, “but I’ve heard folks around here talking about how the A’s keep winning even as players come and go.” They paused, weighing something in their palm. “It’s interesting how they manage to stay strong like that.” Interesting, yes. But what is strength when there’s no alternative? When the structure is designed to stand regardless of who’s holding up the beams? The record doesn’t remember the moments of doubt, the fractures. It only knows the final weight, distributed across whatever—whoever—was available to bear it at the time.

Meanwhile, Irene Fay, a barista from a nearby coffee shop, sat at the end of the bar, looking a bit out of place. "I feel like community engagement with the Oaks team is something I've heard about, but I don't really know much about it. As a barista, I mostly just focus on my job and don't really get involved in that kind of thing," she said, looking around the bar with a curious expression. Darius Clark, a bakery worker and regular at the bar, overheard our conversation and added, "I feel like the community is pretty supportive of the Oaks team, I see people around here talking about them and it seems like they're trying to engage with us more."

Now set that against the Oaks, because Oakland has always held two athletic temperaments at once. Tanya Cruz was in the locker room after another preseason loss, third in a row, and she captured something Hal's column couldn't — the specific silence of a team that hasn't found itself yet. Coen Carr shoulder-checked the door open with 14 points and a jaw that wasn't loosened by any of them. Dame Sarr had three steals and seven points and the arithmetic didn't comfort anyone. Cruz ended on a question — what's waiting for them in the film room — and I think she meant it literally. Some weeks the right move is to name the open question and stop.

What I'm watching next week: whether anyone at the council level responds to the civic gap that two servers named without coordinating. Whether OARI's program managers surface any response to the Civis Systems flag. And whether the A's, at 127 wins and climbing, start to feel the particular pressure of a city that has decided in advance that this story ends with confetti — and whether that expectation is a gift or a weight the team hasn't been asked yet to carry. ============================================================

No one lingered at the showers. The usual post-game chatter died somewhere between the benches and the cold tub. Even the equipment manager moved quieter, stacking damp jerseys like he was handling evidence. What’s waiting for them in the next game’s film room? ============================================================ By Jax Caldera | Bay Tribune Civic The Alert With No Yesterday Lucia Polito is three cars back in the TacoRail line on International, watching the drive-thru crawl slower than she's ever seen it, when she finally says what's been sitting on her for weeks. "I've felt a sense of uncertainty about the Oakland Alternative Response Initiative," she tells me, engine running, wipers going. And when I went looking for the initiative, the task force, the office, the anything with a name on it that's supposed to be sitting on this fire — there's nothing. No matching program. No mitigator. Nobody's desk.

I found Celeste Moon near the towers that stay lit past when anybody's working in them, and she hadn't heard about any of it. "I haven't really thought about it," she said, "but I did hear Downtown was packed last night. That's all I know." Packed. Lit up. And decaying underneath it — those aren't contradictions, they're the same neighborhood wearing two faces depending which number you trust. Then there's Eunice Marston, who runs faith work out of her building and watches her congregation stream past SpeedyBurger every week like clockwork. "I haven't really seen any significant changes or initiatives that address the concerns about Downtown decay," she told me, "but I do see people from my community, like those coming out of Telegraph Presbyterian, going about their daily lives. As a faith leader, I try to stay focused on the people and their needs, rather than getting caught up in the broader issues." That's a pastor telling me, politely, that the city hasn't given her congregation anything to point at either. She's not chasing the broader issues because nobody handed her a broader issue to chase — just a block getting quietly worse under lit windows.

What evidence supports the alert — and who's going to step up and tell Fruitvale, West Oakland, and East Oakland what it's actually measuring?
